SLOW MOTION: 1080p HD slow motion (no AI video) of the impact of a Learjet 60 that crashed in Greenacres, Palm Beach County, Florida, on Sunday, November 1, 2026 at about 12:50 p.m. All nine souls aboard were killed.

I got hold of the public dash cam video and, using professional video software (FFmpeg), upscaled it from its original 720p to 1080p with Lanczos resampling, a standard mathematical scaler. No AI and no made-up frames. Every frame you see came from the camera.

What I did:
- Found the very first frame where the jet's nose comes into view (frame 52 of 417)
- From there to the impact flash, each frame is held for half a second (1/15 speed) so you can see every one
- The fireball plays at half speed, then real time until the driver reacts
- Then a replay of just the plunge and impact at 1/21 speed, 0.7 seconds per frame

I skipped motion interpolation on purpose. The jet was moving so fast it covered a huge distance between frames, and the interpolation software was inventing ghosted, doubled airplanes that never existed. I'd rather show you only what the camera actually caught.

The aircraft was a 22-year-old twin-engine Learjet 60, a mid-size business jet, tail number N722BD. It left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas bound for North Eleuthera in the Bahamas. According to the FAA, it dropped from 35,250 feet to 8,750 feet in a little over a minute, about 350 feet per second. On air traffic control audio, a woman on board can be heard calling mayday and reporting they were descending at 10,000, then 20,000 feet per minute.

It came down beside Military Trail between Cresthaven Blvd and 10th Ave North. There were no early reports of anyone on the ground being hurt. It's still unclear whether the storm played a role. The FAA and NTSB are investigating.

A note on the timestamp: the dash cam reads 13:51, but the crash happened at 12:50 p.m. Daylight saving time ended that morning, and the camera's clock almost certainly never fell back.

My favorite SEO hack

- Go to google search console
- Performance > search results
- Add filter > query > custom (regex)
- Paste this: ^(?:\S+\s+){7,}\S+$
- It shows every search with 8+ words

These are the long, specific questions people google before they find you. it's the same kind of question they ask chatgpt

Pick the ones with high impressions and low clicks, and answer them at the top of the page that ranks

He believes most Steam users simply have no reason to move to another store, even if it offers a better experience.

Ritchie says that Steam has become so dominant that developers can’t afford to ignore it, leaving them with no choice but to accept the 30% cut.
